content: 1. During the transfer of cargo between transport units or between transport units and warehouses, as well as during the removal of items from pallets or overpacks for manual or mechanical handling, it is essential to ensure that the packaging is designed and sealed to prevent any loss of contents. This includes protection against potential leakage caused by vibration, temperature changes, humidity, or pressure variations under normal transport conditions. 2. Packaging must consist of at least three components: a. A primary receptacle, b. A secondary packaging, and c. An outer packaging. Either the secondary or the outer packaging must be rigid, and the outer packaging must always be rigid. 3. Primary receptacles must be securely packed within secondary packaging to ensure that, under normal transport conditions, they do not break, puncture, or leak their contents into the secondary packaging. Secondary packaging must be secured within the outer packaging using appropriate cushioning materials. Any leakage from the contents must not compromise the integrity of the cushioning material or the outer packaging. 4. For transport, the outer packaging must display a clearly visible and legible mark on its external surface. This mark should be on a contrasting background and must be in the form of a diamond-shaped square with each side measuring at least 50 mm. The line width must be at least 2 mm, and the letters and numbers must be at least 6 mm high. The proper shipping name, BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B, must also be marked adjacent to the diamond-shaped mark in letters at least 6 mm high. 5. At least one surface of the outer packaging must have minimum dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm. After undergoing the appropriate drop sequence, there must be no leakage from the primary receptacle(s), which must remain protected by absorbent material (if required) within the secondary packaging. 6. For liquid substances: a. The primary receptacle(s) must be leakproof and must not contain more than 1 liter. b. The secondary packaging must also be leakproof. c. If multiple fragile primary receptacles are placed in a single secondary packaging, they must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact between them. d. Absorbent material must be placed between the primary receptacle(s) and the secondary packaging. e. The outer package must not contain more than 4 liters, excluding ice, dry ice, or liquid nitrogen used for refrigeration. 7. For solid substances: a. The primary receptacle(s) must be siftproof and must not exceed the outer packaging mass limit. b. The secondary packaging must also be siftproof. c. If multiple fragile primary receptacles are placed in a single secondary packaging, they must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact between them. d. Except for packages containing body parts, organs, or whole bodies, the outer package must not contain more than 4 kg, excluding ice, dry ice, or liquid nitrogen used for refrigeration. e. If there is any doubt about the presence of residual liquid in the primary receptacle during transport, packaging suitable for liquids, including absorbent materials, must be used. 8. When ice is used, it must be placed outside the secondary packaging or in the outer packaging or overpack. Interior supports must secure the secondary packaging in its original position. If ice is used, the outer packaging or overpack must be leakproof. The primary receptacle and secondary packaging must maintain their integrity at the temperature of the refrigerant used, as well as at the temperatures and pressures that could result if refrigeration were lost. 9. When packages are placed in an overpack, the required package marks must either be clearly visible or reproduced on the outside of the overpack. 10. Infectious substances assigned to UN 3373 that are packed and marked in accordance with these instructions are not subject to any other requirements in these regulations. 11. Passengers and crew members are prohibited from transporting infectious substances as carry-on baggage, checked baggage, or on their person. 12. For non-infectious specimens containing small quantities of ethanol, formaldehyde solution, or other flammable liquids, specific packing and marking requirements must be met. These include wrapping specimens in absorbent material, sealing them in plastic bags, and placing them in strong outer packaging with appropriate cushioning. The total quantity of flammable liquid per outer packaging must not exceed 1 liter, and the package must be marked with scientific research specimens, not restricted. Special Provision A180 applies. 13. When dry ice is used as a refrigerant, the packaging must allow for the venting of carbon dioxide gas to prevent a dangerous build-up of pressure. Insulated packaging containing refrigerated liquid nitrogen fully absorbed in a porous material is not subject to Dangerous Goods Regulations, provided the design prevents pressure build-up and liquid nitrogen release. 14. For genetically modified microorganisms (GMMOs) and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) packed and marked in accordance with Packing Instruction 959, no additional requirements apply under the Dangerous Goods Regulations. 15. For documentation purposes, the proper shipping name must be supplemented with the technical name, though technical names need not appear on the package itself.
